ety.text: From Middle English hot, hoot, from Old English hāt (“hot”), from Proto-West Germanic *hait, from Proto-Germanic *haitaz (“hot”), from Proto-Indo-European *keHy- (“to heat; to become hot”). Cognates Cognate with Yola hoat, hoate, hote (“hot”), West Frisian hjit, hyt (“hot”), Bavarian hoaß (“hot”), Central Franconian heeß (“hot”), Dutch heet (“hot”), German heiss, heiß, heyß (“hot”), Vilamovian haas, haes, hȧś, hǡs (“hot”), Yiddish הייס (heys, “hot”), Danish hed (“hot”), Faroese and Icelandic heitur (“hot”), Norwegian Bokmål and Swedish het (“hot”); also Lithuanian kaitra (“heat”).

senses.d: Having or giving off a high temperature.
ex: He forgot that the frying pan was hot and burned his hand.
It is too hot to be outside.

senses.d: Feeling the sensation of heat, especially to the point of discomfort.
ex: I was so hot from being in the sun too long.
Aren't you hot with that thick coat on?

senses.d: Feverish; feeling a high fever.
Active, in use or ready for use (like a bullet or a firing range), turned on (like a microphone or camera).
ex: The microphone was hot and the show was on the air.
I run an inventory, verify all bullets are hot in the chamber. They are. But the showroom prosthetics have all exited attraction mode.

senses.d: Electrically charged.
Radioactive.
In active use at or near capacity.
ex: We need to keep the old drone production line going while it's still hot, or it'll be difficult to restart it.

senses.d: Easily provoked to anger.
ex: Be careful, he has a hot temper and may take it out on you.

senses.d: Physically or sexually attractive.
ex: He saw many hot girls at the concert.

senses.d: Sexual or sexy; involving sexual intercourse or sexual excitement.
Hotly; at a high temperature.
Rapidly, quickly.
ex: Whatever happened, braking into the next-to-last hairpin, a blue-sky turn called Cog Cut, Durelle went in too hot.
They were coming in hotter than Dash liked, nose down toward the watery surface […]

senses.d: While shooting, while firing one's weapon(s).
ex: to come in hot; to go in hot

senses.d: To heat; to make or become hot.
To become lively or exciting.
